content:
Pilates can be a good choice for many people with arthritis. It builds core and muscle strength, improves posture, flexibility and balance, and is low impact. It counts as the kind of therapeutic exercise NICE recommends for osteoarthritis and low back pain. Choose a beginners' or clinical class, tell the instructor about your joints, and adapt moves that cause pain.

What Pilates involves

Pilates is a system of controlled exercises that focus on the deep muscles of the tummy, back and pelvis, along with breathing and posture. Classes are done on a mat or on special equipment called reformers. "Clinical Pilates" is run by physiotherapists and is tailored to people with health conditions.

How it can help arthritis

  • stronger muscles around the hips, knees and spine reduce load on painful joints
  • better posture and core control, which can ease back and neck pain
  • improved balance, lowering the risk of falls
  • gentle flexibility work, helping stiff joints move more freely
  • focus on breathing, which helps some people relax and manage pain

NICE recommends exercise, including muscle strengthening and general fitness, as a core treatment for osteoarthritis (NG226) and low back pain (NG59). It does not recommend one type over another, so choose what you enjoy and can keep doing.

Is it safe?

Pilates is generally safe for arthritis when the level is right. Things to watch:

  • Knees: kneeling can be painful. Use a folded mat or cushion, or swap for standing or lying alternatives.
  • Hips: after a hip replacement, avoid bending the hip past 90 degrees or crossing your legs unless your surgeon allows it.
  • Hands and wrists: weight-bearing on the hands, as in plank, can strain sore wrists. Try forearms or a wall instead.
  • Spine and osteoporosis: avoid deep forward bending and twisting moves such as "roll-ups" if you have osteoporosis or a spinal fracture. A clinical Pilates instructor can advise.
  • Neck: if your neck is affected, for example in RA or ankylosing spondylitis, keep your head supported during exercises that lift the head.

Some muscle tiredness the next day is normal. Sharp pain during an exercise, or pain that lasts more than a day, means you should ease off.

Getting started

  • Ask your physiotherapist whether Pilates suits you and which moves to avoid.
  • Look for a beginners' class, a "Pilates for back care" class or a clinical Pilates class.
  • Check the instructor's qualifications, and tell them about your arthritis and any joint replacements.
  • Start with one class a week and build up.
  • Practise a few moves at home between sessions.

Online videos can be useful once you know the basics, but in-person teaching is safer at first.

Simple moves to try

  • Pelvic tilts: lying on your back with knees bent, gently flatten your back into the mat, then release.
  • Knee rolls: in the same position, let your knees sway slowly to one side and back.
  • Clam: lying on your side with knees bent, lift your top knee while keeping feet together. This strengthens the hips.
  • Bridge: lying on your back, lift your hips slowly, then lower.

Do 5 to 10 of each, slowly and with control.

Cost and access

Pilates is not usually offered as standalone NHS treatment, though some NHS physiotherapy services run classes. Private and leisure centre classes vary in cost. Some gyms include classes in membership.

Pilates as part of a balanced routine

Pilates is a good complement to walking, swimming or cycling. Combining it with some aerobic activity gives you the widest benefits for joints, heart and mood.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
